title: The midnight roll call
objectives: Read a YARA-L Search query before building it.
Separate login attempts, allowed logins and failures.
Count different account IDs and event records.
Group job titles only where the logs supply them.
Run queries separately in SecOps; return no workplace observations.
story: MIDNIGHT AT MERIDIAN — Doors open in forty minutes for the planetarium's charity premiere. The donation screen suddenly advertises a private 'VIP orbit pass' nobody approved. Sponsor manager Rafi calls it a rehearsal. Intern Jules gets blamed because he was last seen at the console. Director Mira wants evidence before anyone gets a villain edit. Your first job: establish who could sign in, separate success from failure, and find a defensible account lead. This original case and its clues are authored fiction; workplace searches are separate practice.

teaching.heading: One case, one small move at a time
teaching.text: Read the case question and explanation, then check the training query. You can also run it separately in authorized SecOps. First you get the whole query, then gaps, then independent tasks. Hints are always available.

teaching.heading: An event is one record of something happening
teaching.text: A login record can describe an attempt that worked or failed. A field is a named detail in that record. metadata.event_type is the “what happened?” label. Each mission explains the new pieces before you use them. Two adjacent filter conditions mean both must match (implicit AND). Writing AND explicitly is optional; the next mission shows both forms.

teaching.heading: Set the range in SecOps
teaching.text: Choose manual Search with YARA-L 2.0, then Relative time: 30 Minutes. Keep that range while comparing these queries. Time is a separate Search control; do not add KQL ago() or a detection-rule window to these examples.

teaching.heading: The story is fictional; workplace practice stays private
teaching.text: Case clues are authored fiction, revealed after the query check; they are not derived from workplace results. Keep actual identifiers, records and observations in employer tools. The separate feedback box accepts reviewed course/platform screenshots, never internal data.

teaching.heading: First calculate, then name the output
teaching.text: outcome: starts the returned calculations. In $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid), $users is a chosen output name; count_distinct is the function; the field in parentheses supplies the values to count. The distinct part is in the function's name. Each different nonempty ID counts once.

teaching.heading: A lead is a question, not a culprit
teaching.text: Start with what changed, what system could change it, and which records could test that idea. An account can be shared or stolen. A successful sign-in says access was allowed; it does not identify the human or prove their actions were approved.

challenges.title: Open the login door
challenges.prompt: What login records are available? Select the USER_LOGIN event category. In SecOps, use the last 30 minutes. This first query returns records, not a count.
hints: Choose the normalized event category field, not a raw vendor event code.
Use metadata.event_type, equality, and the quoted USER_LOGIN enum.

methodQuestions.prompt: Which part selects the kind of event?

options.label: metadata.event_type
"USER_LOGIN"
principal.user.userid

methodQuestions.rationale: metadata.event_type is the field path. USER_LOGIN is the value we compare it with.

options.label: The quotes make this a partial-text search.
It is the event-type string value being matched.
The quotes bind the value to an output variable.

methodQuestions.rationale: Quoted text is a string value. The = operator requests equality; it does not make a substring search.

mission.beat: The premiere screen changed without an approved cue. Mira says, 'Start with access, not accusations.' Find login records in the last thirty minutes; do not count anything yet.

explanation.meaning: The event's label card: details that describe the record.
The “what happened?” box on that card. Dots lead through the field path.
Keep only records matching the value on the right.
Google's login-event label. Keep the capitals and quotation marks.

mission.remember: Show me records wearing the login badge.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the publishing console uses a shared show account. Jules being near the keyboard cannot settle who signed in. Next, separate allowed attempts from failed ones.

analystNote.text: A log is a record of activity. An incident is an investigated security problem. USER_LOGIN selects a category; it does not say whether the login worked or was suspicious.

challenges.title: Keep the successful sign-ins
challenges.prompt: Keep USER_LOGIN records and add security_result.action = ALLOW. Return the matching records.
hints: Keep the category and add an action requirement.
Use the quoted ALLOW value. Both filters must hold.

methodQuestions.prompt: What changes when you add the ALLOW condition?

options.label: The query keeps login records whose recorded action is ALLOW.
The query keeps ALLOW records of every event type.
The query keeps all login records and only changes the displayed columns.

methodQuestions.rationale: The two filter conditions both apply; adding a condition narrows the selected records.

methodQuestions.prompt: What happens if AND is omitted between these two filter conditions?

options.label: Both conditions still apply: an implicit AND.
The conditions become OR alternatives.
Only the second condition is applied.

methodQuestions.rationale: Adjacent filter conditions are implicitly joined with AND. Writing AND explicitly is also valid.

mission.beat: Rafi says the VIP screen is impossible because 'the password was rejected.' Mira asks, 'Was every attempt rejected?' Keep the login category and require an allowed action.

explanation.meaning: Keep login-attempt records.
Also require the recorded allowed action. AND means both conditions must match the same record.

metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "ALLOW"
These adjacent filter conditions mean the same thing: an implicit AND. A line break makes it readable; it is not a different operator.
Both forms are valid here. We show AND while introducing filters so the connection is visible. Use OR when either alternative may match; it means something different.

mission.remember: AND keeps both requirements. Writing it out makes the rule visible.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the technician confirms there was a normal rehearsal sign-in as well as rejected attempts. 'Some failures' does not mean 'no access.' Next, count accounts instead of repeated sign-ins.

analystNote.concept: Allowed does not mean authorized business use
analystNote.text: ALLOW records the product's access decision. An approved user, a shared account and stolen credentials can all produce successful authentication. Your next question is whose account and in what context.

challenges.title: Count accounts, not repeated logins
challenges.prompt: Count distinct nonempty principal.user.userid values in ALLOW USER_LOGIN records. Return one count without grouping.
challenges.referenceQuery:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
AND security_result.action = "ALLOW"
AND principal.user.userid != ""
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)
acceptedVariants:
security_result.action = "ALLOW" AND principal.user.userid != "" AND metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
outcome:
  $unique_users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)
hints: The worked example spells out the function: count_distinct. The word distinct is part of its name after the underscore.
Keep principal.user.userid != "" above outcome:, then use $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid).

metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
AND security_result.action = "ALLOW"
AND principal.user.userid != ""
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)

methodQuestions.prompt: Where does this query ask for different account IDs to be counted once?

options.label: In count_distinct(principal.user.userid).
In the output name $users.
In principal.user.userid != "".

methodQuestions.rationale: The full function name is count_distinct. Its _distinct part means duplicate values count once; the field in parentheses specifies which values.

methodQuestions.prompt: What does principal.user.userid != "" do before counting?

options.label: Removes records whose account-ID field is empty.
Removes later logins by an ID already seen.
Creates the $users output column.

methodQuestions.rationale: != means not equal, and "" is an empty string. This filter excludes missing IDs; count_distinct separately handles duplicates.

mission.beat: Mira asks how many different account badges are represented. Ten sign-ins from one shared account should not become ten suspects. Learn the complete counting expression before changing it.
mission.example:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
AND security_result.action = "ALLOW"
AND principal.user.userid != ""
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)
mission.starter:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
AND security_result.action = "ALLOW"
AND principal.user.userid != ""
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)

explanation.meaning: The account ID recorded in the principal role. This is the field whose different values we want to count.
!= means “not equal.” Two quotes with nothing between them mean an empty string. This filter keeps records with a nonempty account ID, so a missing ID is not counted as an extra value.
Start the calculations returned by the search. This query calculates one summary across the filtered records; match would split it into groups.
The output name you choose for the calculated value. The $ prefix marks the variable. It is a label for the count, not a username or a field fetched from a log.
Assign the calculation on the right to the output name on the left. In a filter, = compares a field with a value; here it names a calculated result.

This is where “distinct” appears: inside the function name count_distinct. It counts each different value once. Think ID A, ID A, ID B → two different IDs. KQL's separate distinct operator is not used here.
The parentheses tell count_distinct which field to count. The whole line reads: name this output $users, and calculate the number of different account IDs.

mission.remember: count_distinct is the whole function name. The distinct part is after the underscore.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the show account is shared between a technician and a sponsor operator. Even a correct distinct-account count cannot identify the number of people at the controls.
mission.caveat: This covers only populated IDs in the selected field, not every employee or every human.

analystNote.text: One person may use several accounts; several people may share one account. Count different IDs to describe the records, then use authorized context to investigate ownership.

challenges.title: Which job titles are recorded?
challenges.prompt: For ALLOW USER_LOGIN records, require nonempty principal.user.userid and principal.user.title. Group by principal.user.title and count distinct user IDs within each title.
challenges.referenceQuery:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "ALLOW"
principal.user.userid != ""
principal.user.title != ""
match:
  principal.user.title
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)
acceptedVariants:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "ALLOW"
principal.user.userid != ""
principal.user.title != ""
$title = principal.user.title
match:
  $title
outcome:
  $unique_users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)
hints: Job titles, event roles and system permissions are different concepts.
Keep the successful-login filters, skip missing user/title values, group by title and count distinct user IDs.

metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "ALLOW"
principal.user.userid != ""
principal.user.title != ""
match:
  principal.user.title
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)

options.label: It creates a separate summary group for each recorded title.
It filters to one exact job title.
It changes the counted field from account ID to title.

methodQuestions.rationale: match selects grouping keys. The outcome still counts different account IDs, now within each title group.

methodQuestions.prompt: Which records remain after adding principal.user.title != ""?

options.label: Only matching records with a nonempty recorded title.
All matching records, with missing titles renamed Unknown.
Only records whose title differs from their account ID.

methodQuestions.rationale: The empty-string filter removes blank titles. It does not infer or fill missing titles.

mission.beat: Jules is labelled 'Lighting assistant' on the cue sheet. Rafi is 'Sponsor liaison.' Mira asks which job titles the sign-in records actually carry. Use only populated titles; do not invent a permission map.
mission.example:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "ALLOW"
principal.user.userid != ""
principal.user.title != ""
match:
  principal.user.title
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)
mission.starter:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "ALLOW"
principal.user.userid != ""
principal.user.title != ""
match:
  principal.user.title
outcome:
  $users = count_distinct(principal.user.userid)

explanation.meaning: A recorded job title, not an administrator-permission flag.
Keep records that actually contain a title.
Make one summary group for each different key listed below it.
Use the recorded title as the group label.
Count different account IDs within each title, rather than repeated logins.

mission.remember: Group by the label; count the badges in each group.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the shared publishing account has no useful job title. Jules's job label is context, not proof of publishing permission. Missing enrichment becomes an evidence gap, not a guess.
mission.caveat: Optional workplace capability: many login sources have no job title. If unavailable, continue the course example without inferring a title. This query does not prove a person's authoritative job at that historical time.

analystNote.text: A job title is descriptive context. Authorization comes from permissions and roles on the system. A blank title does not mean an unknown attacker or an unprivileged account.

challenges.title: Count the attempts that failed
challenges.prompt: Count distinct metadata.id values in USER_LOGIN records with FAIL action. Return one count, without grouping or restricting to one account.
hints: Use the login category, the failure action and a summary count.
Count metadata.id, not user IDs; those answer different questions.

methodQuestions.prompt: What changes when the argument becomes metadata.id?

options.label: The calculation counts different event-record IDs.
The calculation counts different account IDs.
The calculation groups the results by event type.

methodQuestions.rationale: The field inside count_distinct controls what is counted. metadata.id identifies a normalized record; principal.user.userid identifies an account.

methodQuestions.prompt: What change would count different failed-login accounts instead of different failed-login records?

options.label: Count principal.user.userid, excluding empty user IDs.
Rename $failures to $users but keep metadata.id inside the function.
Add principal.user.userid under order without changing the outcome.

methodQuestions.rationale: Renaming an output does not change its calculation. Change the argument to count_distinct and exclude empty IDs.

mission.beat: The console operator admits retrying an old password. Rafi calls every rejection 'a brute-force attack.' Count the failed records first; the same tool can answer a different question by changing its argument.

explanation.meaning: The normalized failure action. Verify the product mapping privately.
The normalized record ID. Counting distinct IDs avoids recounting the same ID.
A name for the calculated summary. No actual count is submitted here.
Count different matching records, not different users.

mission.remember: Same counting tool, different thing inside the parentheses.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the operator explains some failures but cannot account for every retry. Keep both stale credentials and unauthorized access as hypotheses. Next, focus on the shared account.
mission.caveat: Separate products can give different record IDs to the same real action. This is not automatically a unique real-world attempt count.

analystNote.text: A wrong saved password, expired credential or automated task can produce failures. Count and scope the activity before calling it brute force. Different event IDs also need not equal different real-world attempts.

challenges.title: Follow one account
challenges.prompt: Select USER_LOGIN records whose principal.user.userid exactly equals [USER]. Keep "__USER__" in the course. Choose and substitute the real account only inside SecOps.
hints: Add an identity constraint to the category filter; both must hold.
The training actor identity field is principal.user.userid. Use [USER] and AND.

methodQuestions.prompt: Which filter keeps the exact principal account requested by the mission?

options.label: principal.user.userid = "__USER__"
target.user.userid = "__USER__"
principal.hostname = "__HOST__"

methodQuestions.rationale: The field path defines the role and detail. target.user.userid can refer to a different account role; hostname is a device field.

methodQuestions.prompt: What happens if the USER_LOGIN condition is removed?

options.label: The query still searches only login records.
The filter changes from the principal role to the target role.
The account filter can match other event types too.

methodQuestions.rationale: Each condition controls part of the scope. The user filter does not imply an event category.

mission.beat: The support ticket identifies the shared publishing account. On this site it is [USER]. Build an exact login query for that account; real values belong only in SecOps.

explanation.meaning: The exact account ID in the actor field requested by this mission.
A training placeholder. Replace it only in workplace SecOps.
Keep the event category attached to the account requirement.

mission.remember: Follow the badge, but keep the event label attached.
mission.caseUpdate: Chapter handoff: access category, outcome, distinct accounts and failed records answer different questions. You have an account lead, not a named culprit. Next, check how that account appears in different roles.
mission.caveat: This task teaches the specified principal role. Inspect and adapt source-specific mappings privately.

analystNote.text: A pivot follows a lead into another scoped search. Keep the event category while adding the account, so unrelated activity does not silently change your investigation.
